Special Relativity: Einstein's special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in a vacuum, c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s, is the same for all observers. Time dilation: a moving clock runs slower, t = gamma t0, where t0 is the proper time and gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2). Length contraction: a moving object is shorter along the direction of motion, L = L0 / gamma. Mass-energy equivalence: E = m c^2; the total energy is E = gamma m c^2 and the kinetic energy is (gamma - 1) m c^2. Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light. Relativity is confirmed by muon decay and by GPS clocks.
Photons and the Photoelectric Effect: Light also behaves as particles called photons, each with energy E = h f = h c / lambda, where h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s is Planck's constant. In the photoelectric effect light shining on a metal ejects electrons only if the frequency is above a threshold frequency f0, however intense the light is. The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons is KE_max = h f - phi, where phi = h f0 is the work function of the metal. Increasing the intensity increases the number of electrons (the current) but not their maximum energy; increasing the frequency increases the energy. The stopping potential satisfies e V_s = KE_max. This effect could not be explained by wave theory and supported the quantum theory of light. It is used in solar cells and light sensors.
Matter Waves and the Bohr Atom: Particles also behave as waves. The de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h / p = h / (m v). Electron diffraction confirmed this. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly: delta x delta p is at least h / (4 pi). In the Bohr model of hydrogen the electron occupies discrete energy levels E_n = -13.6 eV / n^2, n = 1, 2, 3... Light is emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps between levels: h f = E_high - E_low. The wavelengths of the hydrogen spectrum come from these jumps, for example the Balmer series ends at n = 2. The ground state n = 1 has energy -13.6 eV, and the ionization energy is 13.6 eV. In modern quantum mechanics electrons are described by probability waves.
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons (nucleons). A nuclide is written as Z X with mass number A and atomic number Z; isotopes have the same Z but different A. The strong nuclear force holds nucleons together. The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its nucleons; this mass defect gives the binding energy E = delta m c^2 (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2). Unstable nuclei decay: alpha decay emits a helium nucleus (A decreases by 4, Z by 2), beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton and emits an electron (Z increases by 1) and gamma decay emits a photon. Radioactive decay is random but the activity follows N = N0 e^(-lambda t), with half-life T(1/2) = 0.693 / lambda; after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n. Radioactive dating, medicine and power use these ideas.
Fission, Fusion and the Standard Model: In nuclear fission a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing neutrons and about 200 MeV; the neutrons can cause a chain reaction, controlled in reactors and uncontrolled in bombs. In nuclear fusion light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes join to form heavier nuclei, releasing even more energy per kilogram; it powers the Sun but requires temperatures of millions of kelvins. Both release energy because the binding energy per nucleon increases toward iron-56, the most stable nucleus. Matter is built from quarks (up, down, ...) and leptons (electron, neutrino...), and forces are carried by bosons such as the photon, gluon, W and Z. Each particle has an antiparticle, and when they meet they annihilate into energy. Protons and neutrons are made of three quarks.
